top_comments: There's a snowball's chance in hell that they haven't found any cryptographically-relevant results. And given how security averse the NSA has been (they pushed NIST to standardize a backdoored random number generator then paid the RSA company $10 million to use it[1]), I have the feeling that the findings won't be used to strengthen cybersecurity, but as weapons.More reason to invest in crypto agility, I guess. I just hope that they haven't broken all public key crypto, life is hard enough already.[1] https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-security-rsa-idUSBRE9...

For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/).They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

We've seen so much interesting work come out of OpenAI and Anthropic in the last few weeks. It really feels like both have tapped into the pioneering spirit of the old Bell Labs.But, Bell Labs existed as part of an agreement with the government that AT&T's monopoly would be used for the public good. OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have much use for this beyond PR...If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems? Scaring mathematicians into burning their non-existent research budgets on tokens in order to make a couple million dollars?Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude, Copilot, or OpenAI. Unfortunately, the average business doesn't care that the AI can solve frontier problems: they just need something to summarize emails or give an executive a summary of the day's headlines. The market is just waiting for a cheap provider that is just as turnkey... Which isn't exactly a high barrier these days. IMO there is space for a unicorn to emerge in the next few years to eat everyone's lunch.

articles.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
articles.summary: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed

top_comments: This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache.As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question).More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

None of the attacks discussed here are realistic in any way.They require a bunch of extremely improbable conditions to hold, and a huge amount of information on the exact details of the hardware and software stack.- the two agents must be aware of each other and must have pre-shared messages to check - they can't spontaneously discover each other and start communicating in this way- they must know the details of the inference server they are running under and its possible kernels and its limits (what is a "short prompt" vs "a long prompt" for this setup)- they must have a way to run at almost the same time- the prefix cache must have little contention so that their blocks can't be evicted (note: the article mostly talks about KV cache, but it's actually the prefix cache that is relevant here)- the models need either (1) direct access to the numerical results of the inference process, instead of the text that vLLM provides, (2) access to the exact responses that a helper model will produce with the short-kernel numerical results vs the long-kernel numerical results; this is the most critical step that is impossible to reproduce on any common kind of deployment- there must not be any other kind of variability in the system (different GPUs, multiple inference servers behind a load balancer, more complex distributed inference setups)The post also mentions all of these limitations, and that the scheme entirely collapses if any of them don't hold. It's a cool idea, but it's a purely theoretical thing that has 0 real-world implications.

Frontier models today can easily figure this out. The less frontier models as of right now are probably going to take a long horizon session to figure out this type of "side channel" comms. However, posting this in depth step by step on the internet and discussed in open forums like here, now all models definitely know about this trick now.
